listening.title: Riverside Community Pool Swimming Classes
listening.focus: Understanding timetable details, corrections and booking information
listening.script:
Anna: Good morning, Riverside Community Pool, Anna speaking, how can I help you?
Mark: Good morning, Anna. My name is Mark. I'm calling about swimming classes for my children.
Anna: Of course, Mark. How old are your children?
Mark: My daughter Maya is seven, and my son Jon is ten.
Anna: And what is their swimming level?
Mark: Maya is a complete beginner. She has never had lessons before. Jon can swim a short distance but needs to improve.
Anna: For beginners aged six to eight, we have three classes each week. They are on Tuesday and Thursday at four o'clock, and on Saturday morning. The Saturday class was at ten o'clock, but we changed it to ten thirty last week because of staff training.
Mark: Thank you for telling me. Saturday at ten thirty is better for us. How long is each class?
Anna: Every children's class is forty-five minutes long. They are all in the small indoor pool, which is warm and not deep.
Mark: That sounds perfect for Maya. What about Jon? He is ten and at intermediate level.
Anna: For intermediate swimmers aged nine to twelve, we have classes on Monday and Wednesday at five pm, and also on Saturday at eleven thirty am. The teacher is Mr Davis, he is very experienced.
Mark: Wednesday at five pm would work well for Jon. Do we need to bring equipment?
Anna: Just swimming costumes, goggles and a towel. We provide kickboards and noodles. Also, please bring a small lock for the locker.
Mark: I understand. What is the price?
Anna: It is twelve dollars for one class, or forty dollars for four classes together. Many parents choose the four-class option because it saves money.
Mark: We will take the four-class option for both children. How can I book?
Anna: I can book you now. I just need your full name and phone number. Also, please arrive fifteen minutes early on the first day to fill in a registration form at reception.
Mark: Sure, it's Mark Lee, and my number is 555-0148.
Anna: Thank you, Mr Lee. I have booked Maya for the beginner class on Saturday at ten thirty, and Jon for the intermediate class on Wednesday at five pm. We look forward to seeing you.

reading.title: Campus Greenhouse Open Day
reading.focus: Identifying main ideas, examples and practical information
reading.passage:
The campus greenhouse at Greenfield University will open its doors to the public next Saturday. It was built five years ago mainly for biology students to grow plants for their studies. At first, only science students used it, but now students from many subjects and local families visit. The Open Day is a chance for everyone to learn about plants and sustainability.

The greenhouse has two main areas with different climates. The first area is warm and humid. It contains tropical plants such as banana trees and orchids, which need high temperatures and a lot of water. The second area is cooler and dry. It contains plants from dry regions, such as cactus and rosemary herbs. Student volunteers work in both areas every week. They water the plants, check the temperature, and clean the glass roof. During the Open Day, these volunteers will give short guided tours every thirty minutes.

A key purpose of the greenhouse is education. Biology students use it to grow vegetables for experiments. For example, one student group is growing lettuce with less water to test if it can still grow well. Another group is testing how different light levels affect tomato growth. These are useful examples of student research. However, the author's main claim is broader: the greenhouse helps all students, not only biology students, to understand environmental responsibility and to think about sustainable living.

The greenhouse also supports the environment in practical ways. It collects rainwater from its roof and uses it for watering, which saved over 5,000 litres of water last year. It also uses solar panels on the roof to make electricity for heating and lights. In addition, the greenhouse supplies fresh herbs and salad leaves to the university café every week. Because the food travels only a short distance, it reduces transport costs and packaging waste. This shows how a small project can have real environmental benefits.

The Open Day will offer several activities for visitors. At 11 am, there will be a planting workshop for children, where they can plant seeds in a small pot to take home. At 2 pm, there will be a talk about composting and how to make soil from food waste. Entry to the Open Day is free, but visitors must book online in advance. This is because space is limited to 100 people per hour for safety reasons. The greenhouse is open from 10 am to 4 pm, and a free university bus will run every 20 minutes from the city centre to the campus.

Overall, the Open Day is a good opportunity to see how a campus project can teach practical skills, provide fresh food, and encourage greener habits for the future.

exercises.title: Campus Greenhouse Open Day
exercises.focus: Identifying main ideas, examples and practical information
exercises.passage:
The campus greenhouse at Greenfield University will open its doors to the public next Saturday. It was built five years ago mainly for biology students to grow plants for their studies. At first, only science students used it, but now students from many subjects and local families visit. The Open Day is a chance for everyone to learn about plants and sustainability.

The greenhouse has two main areas with different climates. The first area is warm and humid. It contains tropical plants such as banana trees and orchids, which need high temperatures and a lot of water. The second area is cooler and dry. It contains plants from dry regions, such as cactus and rosemary herbs. Student volunteers work in both areas every week. They water the plants, check the temperature, and clean the glass roof. During the Open Day, these volunteers will give short guided tours every thirty minutes.

A key purpose of the greenhouse is education. Biology students use it to grow vegetables for experiments. For example, one student group is growing lettuce with less water to test if it can still grow well. Another group is testing how different light levels affect tomato growth. These are useful examples of student research. However, the author's main claim is broader: the greenhouse helps all students, not only biology students, to understand environmental responsibility and to think about sustainable living.

The greenhouse also supports the environment in practical ways. It collects rainwater from its roof and uses it for watering, which saved over 5,000 litres of water last year. It also uses solar panels on the roof to make electricity for heating and lights. In addition, the greenhouse supplies fresh herbs and salad leaves to the university café every week. Because the food travels only a short distance, it reduces transport costs and packaging waste. This shows how a small project can have real environmental benefits.

The Open Day will offer several activities for visitors. At 11 am, there will be a planting workshop for children, where they can plant seeds in a small pot to take home. At 2 pm, there will be a talk about composting and how to make soil from food waste. Entry to the Open Day is free, but visitors must book online in advance. This is because space is limited to 100 people per hour for safety reasons. The greenhouse is open from 10 am to 4 pm, and a free university bus will run every 20 minutes from the city centre to the campus.

Overall, the Open Day is a good opportunity to see how a campus project can teach practical skills, provide fresh food, and encourage greener habits for the future.
exercises.prompt: Why was the greenhouse first built?
exercises.explanation: The passage says it was built mainly for biology students to grow plants. Families visiting came later, so that distractor is incorrect.

writingPrompts.focus: Describing clear main ideas and direct comparisons from a table
writingPrompts.prompt:
The table below shows the results of a student-club bake sale on 15 March at Greenfield College. It shows the price of each item, how many were made, how many were sold, and the total money raised.

Cookies | Price $1.50 | Made 80 | Sold 72 | Raised $108
Brownies | Price $2.00 | Made 60 | Sold 45 | Raised $90
Cupcakes | Price $2.50 | Made 50 | Sold 48 | Raised $120
Lemon Bars | Price $1.00 | Made 40 | Sold 30 | Raised $30

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 1 · Campus Printing Queue Bar Chart
writingPrompts.focus: Reporting main trends and simple comparisons across time
writingPrompts.prompt:
The bar chart below shows the average number of students waiting in the campus printing queue at four times of day on Monday and Friday in the second week of October.

Monday: 9 a.m. 4 students, 12 p.m. 12 students, 3 p.m. 8 students, 6 p.m. 3 students.
Friday: 9 a.m. 2 students, 12 p.m. 6 students, 3 p.m. 5 students, 6 p.m. 1 student.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Beginner Classes at Local Sports Centres
writingPrompts.focus: Presenting clear main ideas with simple reasons and examples
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people think that beginner classes at local sports centres, such as swimming or badminton, are a good way for students to stay healthy and meet new people. Others think students are too busy with study to join these classes.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Waiting Times for Campus Services
writingPrompts.focus: Explaining causes and suggesting simple solutions
writingPrompts.prompt:
At many colleges, students have to wait a long time to use the campus printing service, especially around midday. This wastes time and causes stress.

What do you think are the causes of this problem? What can colleges and students do to reduce waiting times? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

writingPrompts.focus: Expressing an opinion with direct evidence and clear organisation
writingPrompts.prompt:
Some people believe student clubs should raise their own money through activities like bake sales and small events. Others believe colleges should provide all the money clubs need.

Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 1 · Daily Life and Campus Services
speakingPrompts.focus: Talking about familiar routines and simple preferences
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Answer the following questions about your daily life. Give short, clear answers with a reason or example where you can.
1. Do you often need to print documents for your studies?
2. Where do you usually study on campus?
3. How do you usually spend your lunch break?
4. Do you prefer to study alone or with other students? Why?

speakingPrompts.focus: Describing familiar experiences with simple details
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Answer the following questions about food and events. Give short, clear answers with a reason or example where you can.
1. Do you enjoy baking or cooking at home?
2. Have you ever been to a bake sale or food fair at school?
3. What kind of small events do students enjoy at your college?
4. Do you prefer buying snacks or making them yourself? Why?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card · A Beginner Class You Attended
speakingPrompts.focus: Describing an experience in clear order with simple explanation
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Describe a beginner class you attended at a local sports centre or college. You should say:
• what the class was
• where and when it was
• who was in the class with you
• why you decided to join it
and explain what you learned from the class and how you felt about it. You will have one minute to prepare and should speak for one to two minutes.

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Organising Student Events and Clubs
speakingPrompts.focus: Evaluating advantages and giving reasons for opinions
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Consider the following questions about student clubs and events. Give reasons and examples to support your ideas.
1. Why do colleges support student clubs to organise events like bake sales?
2. What are the advantages of learning new skills outside the classroom?
3. Should colleges give money to clubs or should clubs raise money themselves? Why?
4. Do small campus events help students make friends? In what ways?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 3 · Waiting Times and Time Management
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Consider the following questions about waiting and managing time on campus. Give reasons and examples to support your ideas.
1. Why do students have to wait a long time for services like printing at certain times of day?
2. What can colleges do to reduce queues for campus services?
3. Is it better to book a service online or wait in a queue? Why?
4. How does waiting a long time affect students’ study and stress?
